title: Surviving Ancient Skull Surgery 🧠
hook_sentence: Trepanation is the oldest documented surgical procedure in human history, dating back between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago.
narration_script: Trepanation is the oldest documented surgical procedure in human history, dating back between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago. Ancient Peruvian surgeons demonstrated advanced technique by avoiding the midline of the skull, which prevented lethal damage to the cerebral sagittal sinus. Physical evidence suggests prehistoric trepanation served as emergency surgery following trauma to extract shattered bone fragments and clean out pooling blood. Ancient societies also operated for spiritual motives such as releasing evil spirits, or treating mental disorders and epilepsy. By one estimate, advancements in Peruvian surgical technique contributed to cranial surgery survival rates climbing over time to 80 percent. Signs of the bone healing process confirm that patients survived.
closing_sentence: Signs of the bone healing process confirm that patients survived.
caption:
Long before modern operating rooms, prehistoric healers performed ancient cranial surgery 🌿

By one estimate, across various areas of Peru, ancient trepanned skulls were discovered at unusually high rates, representing between 11 and 40 percent of recovered crania. Many of these delicate interventions were performed after cranial trauma caused by prehistoric weapons capable of inflicting severe fractures. Would you have trusted an ancient surgeon with a flint blade? 💭

audits.claim: Trepanation is the oldest documented surgical procedure in human history, dating back between 7,000 and 10,000 years ago.
audits.note: Quote 1 states trepanation dates back to 7,000–10,000 years ago and is perhaps the oldest surgical procedure with archaeological evidence, while Quote 2 identifies it as the oldest documented surgical procedure performed by man.

audits.claim: Ancient Peruvian surgeons avoided the midline of the skull, reducing damage to the cerebral sagittal sinus.
audits.note: Quote 16 and Quote 17 confirm that instruments and techniques in Peru were advanced due to skulls missing the midline, which reduced damage to the cerebral sagittal sinus.

audits.claim: Evidence suggests prehistoric trepanation served as emergency surgery following head wounds to extract shattered bone fragments and clean out pooling blood.
audits.note: Quote 10 states evidence suggests trepanation was primitive emergency surgery after head wounds to remove shattered bits of bone and clean out blood pooling under the skull.

audits.claim: Ancient societies performed trepanation for spiritual purposes such as releasing evil spirits, as well as treating epilepsy and mental disorders.
audits.note: Quote 12 states some ancient societies believed it released evil spirits, and Quote 13 notes primary theories include spiritual purposes and treatment for epilepsy, head wounds, and mental disorders.

audits.claim: Peruvian trepanation survival rates increased over time to 80 percent.
audits.note: Quote 18 states this reflects the improvement in the survival rate increasing over time to 80%.

audits.claim: Across various areas of Peru, between 11 and 40 percent of found skulls exhibited trepanation.
audits.note: Quote 14 and Quote 15 confirm that the rate of skulls found in Peru was significantly high, with between 11 and 40% of skulls found throughout different parts of the area.

audits.claim: Trepanations appear to have been most common in areas where weapons that could produce skull fractures were used.
audits.note: Quote 11 confirms trepanations appear to have been most common in areas where weapons capable of producing skull fractures were used.

audits.claim: At a burial site in France dated to 6500 BCE, 40 out of 120 prehistoric skulls had trepanation holes, with around 40 percent of people surviving the procedure.
audits.note: Quote 6 notes 40 out of 120 prehistoric skulls at a burial site in France dated to 6500 BCE had trepanation holes, and Quote 7 states that at the time only around 40% of people survived the procedure.

audits.claim: Archaeologists identify a trephined skull using the shape of the hole, the cutting edges, and the healing process.
